extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv coaches, and improvisation students
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative principles for creating compelling improv scenes (especially comedic), with emphasis on emotional change, status work, and responsible content choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: A changes B
rubrics_metrics.description: "A changes B." If one character is altered by another, we perceive this as action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core principle: action equals change in characters. Anti-pattern: characters remain unaltered and the audience feels nothing is happening. Examples: Macbeth's emotional content makes the play meaningful; Banquo's ghost and Lady Macbeth's bloodstains dramatize emotional cost; Empire Strikes Back is powerful because of Luke's anguished reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reactions / emotional changes are the heart and soul of stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Reactions, emotional changes, are the heart and soul of stories — what events do to characters matters more than a bare list of plot events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing stories focus on how events affect characters. Even in comedy, strong emotional reactions (often to trivial events) drive interest. If events have no emotional impact on characters, scenes feel thin or empty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: big reactions to little events
rubrics_metrics.description: Most comedy involves people having big reactions to little events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use trivial catalysts (e.g., reading a book, hanging a picture) to prompt hysterical outbursts. Avoid inventing ludicrous events and barely reacting—this squanders the audience's interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must care (raise stakes by showing care)
rubrics_metrics.description: What raising the stakes really means is how much the characters care about the plot — once characters care, it's easy to change them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters emotionally invested so the audience cares about outcomes. If characters don't care or appear ‘cool’, the drama/comedy drains away.

rubrics_metrics.name: React to extraordinary offers
rubrics_metrics.description: If you fail to react to an extraordinary offer, you squander an opportunity to start the story and signal 'the story hasn't begun yet.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to react early forces later offers to be even more extraordinary or loses the audience. Example anti-pattern: an alien revelation met with a shrug leads to audience disengagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always Be Changing (ABC)
rubrics_metrics.description: ABC: Always Be Changing — change (especially emotional change) is interesting; keep changing to remain riveting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sustained, unvarying emotion; if characters remain at the same emotional level the audience will lose interest. Changes can be small but continual and in the same direction to create a satisfying arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status Switch (platform then change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with one improviser high status, the other low status, and over the scene switch the statuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set a clear platform (e.g., job interview), establish and maintain statuses for a while, then provoke and justify a status change. Practical steps: name the job, keep statuses constant, freeze and coach to prompt a drop/rise, use physical adjustments (standing, abasing) to signal status shifts. Variations: reverse roles, silent play, different job choices. Ending with reincorporation strengthens the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jump and justify
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'jump and justify' so that the effect (a shift) can precede the cause, but the cause must be present — the shift must be justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both parts (jump and justify) must be deployed by someone in the scene. Justifications needn't be brilliant, but they must be comprehensive enough to convince the audience; add detail to make feeble justifications convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify emotional reactions (comprehensive detail helps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justifications for changes must be present and sufficiently convincing; weak justifications can become convincing with added detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If emotional overreactions aren't justified, the result is mere shouting or incoherence. Coaches should prompt improvisers to add concrete detail to their justifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show status, don't only say it
rubrics_metrics.description: Low status (or high status) must be performed — not merely described in dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delivery matters: weak lines must be delivered wretchedly to register low status; low-status content spoken confidently reads as arrogance. Use posture, tone, and physicality to convey status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'that's not good enough' resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisers (especially high-status ones) may control or move the scene on with 'So, tell me about...' when inspiration runs dry, which undermines a developing status change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist the urge to move on; if your partner has revealed a way to hurt them, pursue it. Allow the platform to be broken and explored rather than shrinking from discomfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't slosh back and forth — change in one direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Change should move consistently rather than oscillating across the status spectrum ('sloshing back and forth' is a version of 'that's not good enough').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent directional change lets the audience get a handle on what the story is about; indecisive reversals prevent development and bore viewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reincorporation/reincorporation for satisfying endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Reincorporation (bringing earlier material back) or completing the status switch often gives the scene a satisfying sense of story-completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A line or motif returned at the end signals transformation and closure (example: Dom's reincorporation of Claire's line in the bakery job scene).

rubrics_metrics.name: Take responsibility for content; avoid gratuitous mockery
rubrics_metrics.description: Every story has a moral; audiences unconsciously take away a message. Improvisers should be aware of the messages they send rather than throwing away objectionable behavior unexamined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid scenes that mock marginalized people without consequence or change. Offer alternatives that change the moral (e.g., deaf girl turns out to be aware and embarrasses mockers; mockers learn and change; later scenes flip perspective). Beginners may need permission not to censor, but performers onstage must take joint responsibility for content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edgy or satirical material should have a point
rubrics_metrics.description: Being 'edgy' is not an excuse for thoughtless nastiness — great edgy comedy has a clear satirical point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples like South Park: creators make vitriolic observations but always 'know what they're saying.' If performers can't articulate the point, the work likely amounts to relinquishing responsibility rather than satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make offers that elicit big emotions; if partner doesn't respond, react to their lack of emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Make offers designed to provoke emotional change in others; if they fail to respond, be emotional about their callous lack of emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises (e.g., pretend-drunk play, Emo-Roller, It's Tuesday) can give permission to explore larger emotional states. Coaches should praise sustained, serious emotional work rather than letting players default to jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude: play changes with truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in stunt-heavy or exaggerated genres, small believable changes (played with verisimilitude) make dramatic or comic moments powerful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle can distract from hunger for story; the best action or stunt scenes still make the audience care about the chase by believable reactions. Even cartoonish exaggeration must register as emotional change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physicality (posture, movement) to effect status shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct improvisers to change physical stance when changing status (stand up, abase on the floor, hands in face, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical changes make status shifts legible and potent. Coaches can instruct dominant players to adopt more dominant postures and victims to abase themselves as the scene nears closure.
